newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, rebels say crisis talks creeping forward.
newsitem.headline: Peru, rebels say crisis talks creeping forward.

text.p: Negotiations to end Peru's 16- week-old hostage crisis have been slowly advancing, government and Marxist rebel sources said, although the threat still loomed of a violent end to the standoff.
Despite deadlock over the the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's (MRTA) main demand for the freedom of about 450 jailed comrades, both sides acknowledged on Tuesday that progress was being made.
"There are advances. I think this could end in a relatively short time," a government source told Reuters. "It could end sooner than people think."
The source, who asked not to be identified, declined to put a specific timeframe on the end of the crisis.
The source also stressed that the government had no intention of releasing MRTA prisoners in exchange for the 72 VIP hostages who have been held in the Japanese ambassador's home for 112 days.
"We will not cave in, we will not free the MRTA inmates," he said.
MRTA spokesman Isaac Velazco, speaking to Reuters by telephone from Germany, agreed that talks to end Latin America's longest hostage siege were edging forward.
"Important advances have been made," Velazco said. "We take five steps forward, then 10 steps back, then three steps forward again. It takes a lot of patience."
The two sides have not met face to face since March 12, leading the rebels to suspect that President Alberto Fujimori's government may be preparing to end the standoff through force.

"Right now, there is a real danger of intervention" by armed forces in a bid to free the captives, Velazco said. "Chances that the government opts for a military solution or for negotiations are 50-50."
But the government source said storming the residence was extremely unlikely unless the rebels harmed one of the captives.
"If they touch one of the hostages -- even with a rose petal -- then that changes things," he said.

A crack team of 20 heavily armed rebels, led by MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, burst into a cocktail party thrown by Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki on Dec. 17 and took more than 500 guests hostage.

Most of the captives were released but the rebels hung onto those they considered their best bargaining chips including Aoki, two Peruvian government ministers, Fujimori's brother, the Bolivian ambassador and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
Many of the MRTA rebels are teenagers, and some have shown signs of cracking, the government source said.
"Some of the youngsters have practically become hostages. They are becoming impatient that it ends and there's the possibility of desertions," he said.
But Velazco disputed that, saying, "Even if they have to stay put for ... a year or two, rest assured their morale will not give in," he said.

With talks between Cerpa and government negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, on hold for three weeks, a three-man team of mediators has shouldered the burden of maintaining contact with the rebels and preparing the ground for fresh talks.

Vatican representative Juan Luis Cipriani discussed the crisis Tuesday morning for two hours with Fujimori and Palermo. He later met with fellow mediators Red Cross representative Michel Minnig and Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, who returned from a two-day visit to Bolivia on Tuesday.
Cipriani told reporters after the meeting that negotiations would remain shrouded in secrecy for the timebeing.
"We have entered a stage of greater secrecy than before so we cannot give any special information," he said.
